title: Can, want, must, may
goal: Use the six helper verbs that unlock everyday conversation — and discover that the second verb after them stands bare, with no *att*.
bekal: kan, vill, måste, ska, får, bör — their meanings and forms
the rule: after a helper verb, the second verb takes no *att*
asking, offering and saying no politely

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Reglerna i korridoren
dialogs.intro: Ahmad tapes a sheet of paper to the kitchen door. Dian reads it, frowning.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad är det där för papper?
lines.literal: what is it there for paper?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.id: The corridor rules. You have to read them.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Do I have to? What does it say?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Man får inte diska på natten. Och man ska städa varje vecka.
lines.id: You're not allowed to do the dishes at night. And you have to clean every week.
lines.literal: one may not wash-dishes on night-the. and one shall clean every week.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Kan jag städa på söndag istället?
lines.id: Can I clean on Sunday instead?
lines.literal: can I clean on Sunday instead?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Visst. Men du ska skriva ditt namn på listan.
lines.id: Sure. But you need to write your name on the list.
lines.literal: sure. but you shall write your name on list-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag vill gärna hjälpa till. Får jag använda dammsugaren?
lines.id: I'd be glad to help out. May I use the vacuum cleaner?
lines.literal: I want gladly help to. may I use vacuum-cleaner-the?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ja, den står i skåpet. Men du bör fråga Elin först.
lines.id: Yes, it's in the closet. But you should ask Elin first.
lines.literal: yes, it stands in closet-the. but you should ask Elin first.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Den går sönder ibland. Hon kan laga den.
lines.id: It breaks down sometimes. She knows how to fix it.
lines.literal: it goes broken sometimes. she can fix it.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Okej. Då ska jag prata med henne ikväll.
lines.id: Okay. Then I'll talk to her tonight.
lines.literal: okay. then shall I talk with her tonight.

notes: **After a helper verb, the second verb stands bare.** *Du måste **läsa*** — not *du måste att läsa*. Good news: Swedish drops *att* in exactly the places English drops *to* (*you must read*, not *you must to read*; *I can swim*, not *I can to swim*). The rule holds for all six helper verbs in this unit.

**Man får inte** means "you're not allowed to", not "you can't". *Få* with *inte* is always about **permission**, not ability. For "can't", the right word is *kan inte*: *jag kan inte simma* (I can't swim) vs *jag får inte simma* (I'm not allowed to swim). It's the old English "can" vs "may" distinction — except Swedes actually keep it.

**Ska vs måste.** *Måste* is an obligation from outside that can't be negotiated (*jag måste jobba imorgon*). *Ska* is softer: a plan, an agreement, or a rule everyone has signed up to (*du ska städa varje vecka*). If in doubt, *måste* always works and won't be misunderstood. One trap for English speakers: *måste* looks like "must", but *måste inte* means "don't have to", not "must not". For "must not", use *får inte*.

**Bör** means "should, ought to" — advice, not an order. It's gentler than *ska* and much gentler than *måste*. On Swedish notice boards you'll often see all three side by side, and the difference really is noticed.

**Går sönder** — "breaks", literally "goes broken". It's one of those combinations that won't translate word for word; learn it as a whole. English does something similar with "goes wrong" or "breaks down". Its cousins: *går bra* (goes well), *går inte* (can't be done, won't work).

**Vad är det där för papper?** — the pattern *vad… för…* means "what kind of…?". *Vad är det för bok?* (what book is that?), *Vad är det för fel?* (what's wrong?). The *för* part always comes after the verb, right before the noun, and this sounds far more natural than *vilken sorts*.

grammars.title: Six helper verbs
after: Look at the first column: **kan, vill, måste, ska, får, bör** — each has a single form for every person, just like all other Swedish verbs. And none of them ends in *-ar* or *-er*, so you can spot them from a distance. Notice how close several are to English: *kan* ~ can, *vill* ~ will, *måste* ~ must, *ska* ~ shall.

**Måste has no living base form.** In the past, Swedes use *var tvungen att…* ("was forced to") or simply keep *måste* as it is, which in conversation often doubles as past tense too. At A1, use *måste* and don't worry.

**Vill ha** is a pair to learn as a unit: *vill* on its own means "want to do", but "want to have something" is *vill **ha***. *Jag vill ha kaffe* (I'd like coffee) — not *jag vill kaffe*, which is wrong. And beware the false friend: *vill* looks like English "will", but it means "want". "I will" (future) is *jag ska*.

grammars.title: Word order with helper verbs
body: The helper verb takes second place; the main verb waits further back, after the subject and after *inte*.
after: Look at the last row: when **three** verbs stand in a row, only the first one is the helper; the second and third stay in the base form. *Jag vill börja jobba*, *Du måste sluta röka*.

**Inte** always sits after the helper verb and before the main verb: *jag kan inte komma*, *hon vill inte äta* — exactly like English "I can *not* come". Worth remembering, because the position differs from a sentence without a helper (*jag kommer inte*, "I come not").

blocks.text: Swedish famously has no word for "please". There's no direct equivalent. Instead, the politeness lives in **how you build the sentence** and in the word *tack*.

**Nej tack** is a complete and perfectly polite refusal; there's no need to add a long explanation. Swedes really do take one no as a no, and they won't insist or ask again. If you actually want something but say no just to be polite, you won't be offered it a second time.

blocks.title: Ten kinds of tack
items: **Tack** — thanks · **Tack så mycket** — thank you very much · **Tusen tack** — a thousand thanks
**Tack ska du ha** — thanks a lot (warm, very Swedish)
**Tack för idag** — thanks for today (said when leaving a class or meeting)
**Tack för maten** — thanks for the meal; you **must** say it after eating at someone's home. Skipping it really does get noticed.
**Tack detsamma** — thanks, you too (in reply to a good wish)

sections.title: Rules and permission: the language of notice boards

blocks.text: These sentences are posted on the walls of dorms, shared kitchens and public places all over Sweden. You'll be reading them every day.

head: Svenska
English
rows: You must book the laundry room.

blocks.text: **Tvättstugan** — the shared laundry room — deserves a note of its own. Almost every Swedish apartment building has one, and you book your slot on a schedule board or in an app. Using it outside your slot, or leaving it dirty, is one of the most serious social offenses a newcomer to Sweden can commit. This is not a joke.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 6
items: Say these five times from memory: 06.30, 08.15, 11.45, 14.25, 19.35.
Then combine them with this unit's helper verbs: *Jag måste vakna klockan…*, *Vi ska äta klockan…*, *Tåget ska gå kvart över…*
Finally, ask for three kinds of permission: may I come in, may I sit here, may I borrow the vacuum cleaner.
